narrative_purpose: Shows the 'not quite' principle on Earth: three fast swimmers converged on one body, but their tails betray three different ancestries, so the reader sees that convergence drags an anchor of history.
subject: Three streamlined fast-swimming animals shown in side profile, stacked or arrayed across the frame at matched scale so their near-identical torpedo bodies line up. TOP: a shark, its tail a vertical fin that beats side to side. MIDDLE: an extinct ichthyosaur, also with a vertical tail fin. BOTTOM: a dolphin, its tail a horizontal fluke that beats up and down. The bodies are almost the same shape; the tails are visibly oriented differently, the key contrast.
scene: Plain dim teal water, faint light shafts from above, uncluttered so the bodies and tails dominate.
camera: Matched side-on views, all three at the same scale and orientation for direct comparison.
light: Soft cool light from above through water, even on all three; backgrounds dark.
palette: Ocean teal and indigo water, the three animals in cool desaturated tones, no warm accent.
style: Three matched naturalist plates, painterly, reading as a comparison by arrangement.
detail_level: High on the body outlines and especially the tails; minimal background.
composition: Three horizontal animals aligned vertically, the tails grouped toward one side so the orientation difference is easy to compare, dark margins for callouts.
consistency_notes: Real Earth animals, naturalistic. The teaching point is tail orientation, so keep tails clearly readable.
negative_prompt: no text, no lettering, no numbers, no labels, no arrows, no leader lines, no photographic or 3D-render look
